title: Diary Of A CEO Is Making You Less Successful - Barry's Economics
summary: Essay arguing success podcasts mislead: confident experts forecast worst, guests are survivors, luck dominates outcomes, and the format monetizes listener anxiety.

assertions.quote: those experts, they were all actually the worst, the least accurate.

verdicts.note: Tetlock's long-run forecasting study found hedgehog-style confident experts less accurate than fox-style ones.

assertions.quote: the less you know about something, the more confident you are that you understand it

verdicts.note: Dunning-Kruger overconfidence partly replicates but much of the effect is statistical regression; it does not show loud advisers are wrong.

assertions.quote: quality creates a floor and a ceiling. You've got to be able to make music, make good music. But within that range, pure randomness.

verdicts.note: Agent-based toy model only: with Gaussian talent and multiplicative luck, the talent of top performers peaks near 0.66 and falls for higher talent, so the model's authors conclude luck matters more than talent at very high success levels; the underestimation of luck is taken from the cited literature, not modelled.

assertions.quote: from inside success, luck becomes invisible

verdicts.note: Hindsight bias and confabulation are documented, but it is not shown that success stories are mostly rationalization.

Introduction summarises Taleb, Frank and Watts: luck's role is almost always underestimated by successful people because randomness is subtle and narratives of inevitable success are easy to construct (narrative fallacy, hindsight bias); literature review, not a result of the paper.

assertions.quote: We never interview, never interview the thousands of people that also woke up at 5:00 a.m., did the cold plunges, read the books
About 25% of businesses fail in their first year. 40% after 3 years, and half of businesses fail after 5 years.
they need you to stay anxious so that you keep listening

verdicts.note: An argument about incentives and intent, not a measurable claim.
